newsitem.title: USA: CME asks CFTC for wider stock futures price limits.
newsitem.headline: CME asks CFTC for wider stock futures price limits.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange has asked the Commodity Futures Trading Commission for permission to expand daily price limits for CME's seven stock index futures contracts, a CME spokeswoman said Monday.
The CME proposed modifying its price limits, which it most recently changed last July, to reflect planned changes by the New York Stock Exchange in its circuit breakers, she said.

The CME's proposed changes mainly would allow stock index futures contracts to fall further before various curbs take effect, including increasing to 90 points from 70 the maximium amount Standard & Poor's 500 futures can drop in a day.
The changes also would remove the upper daily limit that currently restricts rises in S&P 500 futures to 70 points, allowing potentially unlimited rallies.
The CME's proposal would limit opening price rises or drops, during the first 10 minutes of pit trading in S&P 500 futures, to seven points versus the current five points.
The opening limit still will not apply when futures end the GLOBEX trading session up or down more than seven points, and the GLOBEX price limit would expand to up or down 15 points from 12 points.
The first intermediate down pit limit for S&P 500s would expand to 15 points from current 12-point initial down limit.
The next limit still would kick in when S&P futures fall 30 points, or 250 points in the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
The CME proposed a third intermediate limit when S&P 500 futures drop 45 points, or about 350 points in DJIA, compared to a second current intermediate limit of down 50 points.
The current maximum daily limit of up or down 70 S&P points would become the fourth intermediate down limit, and 90 points would restrict total price drops each day under the proposal.
The CME's price limits are in effect for various lengths of time, some of which would change under the plan, and some limits are tied to coordinated curbs and halts at the NYSE.
As stock futures prices have risen, limits that are measured in points are hit more often and faster than a few years ago even though the percentage change of such moves is smaller.
The CME expects the CFTC to decide on the plan, which includes changes for its six other stock futures, by late January.
The newest plan is part of the CME's efforts implemented after the 1987 stock market crash to keep its stock index futures prices limits coordinated with curbs at the NYSE.

"I wouldn't characterize it (the plan) as a jolt or surprise," she said. "We have been in discussions with the New York Stock Exchange and other market participants for a long time." ((DerivativesDesk(312)408-8750/E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com))
